I ate a lot of varieties, but I'm no expert and don't remember much about them, so please go and buy some yourself~ Generally speaking, green grapes can nearly all be eaten with the skin on, and most are seedless. ＊I bought most of mine at a local shop called "Sanchi Chokusou Furubejipo", which had more than ten varieties at the time, so many Shine Muscat grown in Himeji Oriental Star: grown in small quantities around Japan, oval-shaped, can be eaten with the skin but the skin is noticeable. Other grape varieties Persimmons: persimmons are also an autumn fruit, and there are so many persimmon trees along the roads, full of fruit, giving you wicked thoughts. Later a Japanese person told me "you can pick them freely~", so I tried picking at a spot where the persimmon tree didn't seem to belong to anyone, and they were as good as the ones you pay for! The most common is Fuyu, and there's also Fude persimmon. When you cut open a Fude persimmon the inside is a dark orange that looks like it's gone bad, and that's normal. If you see houses drying persimmons, they're mostly astringent varieties (like "Mino persimmon / shibugaki") meant only for drying and can't be eaten raw, and farm co-op supermarkets usually label them with a warning. A Fude persimmon that looks like it's gone bad Taishu persimmon Chestnuts: the chestnuts common in Japan are big. Sometimes you run into little stalls roasting chestnuts, and the thin astringent skin clinging to the flesh is super hard to peel. Japanese people said you can eat it with the skin and don't need to peel it clean. Water bamboo and a giant pumpkin Conclusion Himeji Castle + Engyoji are a must. A quick trip could do one in the morning and one in the afternoon (2 to 3 hours each), but I'm old, and I can only fit one thing into a day. If you happen to go in mid-October, I strongly recommend watching the "Nada no Kenka Matsuri", and the transport is convenient too. Autumn really is the season of appetite, and not seriously eating the seasonal local produce would be a disservice to yourself.

title: Shodoshima on the Seto Inland Sea, with No Art Festival
abstract: On my way to my next work-exchange spot in Himeji, I stopped by Shodoshima: a three-hour ferry from Himeji Port, a cozy guesthouse, and a soy sauce factory and sake brewery, and only then did I realize it wasn't art festival season at all.
text: Before heading to my next work-exchange spot (Himeji), the Setouchi Triennale was on this year for the first time in a while, so I stopped by Shodoshima for a trip. I'd never taken a ferry and wanted to try one. I'd planned to leave from Kobe and even considered an overnight sailing to save on accommodation, but it happened to be on a ferry maintenance day, so I switched to leaving from Himeji Port, a 3-hour trip. Buses on Shodoshima aren't very frequent, and I had to transfer too, so I left Himeji by boat a bit after 11 and didn't reach my lodging on Shodoshima until 4 or 5 in the afternoon. Sen Guesthouse The place I chose is a home that doubles as a guesthouse, with a kitchen, a living room and a balcony, decorated very cozily, and there's even a hammock by the sea a short walk away. The dorm room had only 4 beds, and I wasn't bothered by roommates at all these days, so it was very peaceful and comfortable. Having just come off a week of nonstop, intense socializing, cooking and wandering around at random were truly the best rest for me. Making breakfast and dinner for myself every day, and even going out on trips, felt too heavy for me these days. On my last evening I met another guest, a Brazilian girl named Hanna, and we soaked our feet, shared dinner and said goodbye to Shodoshima together. Another day, while waiting for a bus, an elderly couple who had retired and moved to Shodoshima gave me a ride. Thank you to the lovely, kind people of once-in-a-lifetime encounters. Notes From about 4,000 yen per person Near the Twenty-Four Eyes Movie Village, and rather hard to reach (though you can ask the bus driver to stop at the guesthouse door, which is already very convenient). You also have to climb about two stories of stairs to get to the house. Update: this summer (2026) they actually installed a cargo lift on the stairs...! @senguesthouse It's not art festival season, huh The funny thing is that only on the night I arrived, while planning where to go the next day, did I realize it wasn't the art festival period at all right then. (The Setouchi Triennale has spring, summer and autumn sessions, with a stretch of non-exhibition time between each.) It was a total blunder, but there were more places to go than I expected (though some spots I found pretty ordinary), and I didn't even go to the farther parts of the island (I was really tired). I visited all the sightseeing spots I should have, but what I liked most was still wandering through small alleys and zoning out. Meiro no Machi and the Angel Road It's in Tonosho, next to the "Dobuchi Strait". As a lover of poking around narrow alleys, I really liked it! This area has some festival art sites (though they were all closed when I went), plus quite a few restaurants and cafés, good for eating and resting. On the way to the seaside spot "Angel Road", I also liked passing Saiko-ji Temple (in May 2026 they welcomed a branch image of Mazu from Beigang Chaotian Temple! So cool!), where you can look out over the town and the sea from above. Twenty-Four Eyes Movie Village and Olive Park Twenty-Four Eyes Movie Village: a village built for filming a movie and then kept, where you can feel the atmosphere of an early Showa fishing village. I'd already been to quite a few rural places and different kinds of buildings, so it was only moderately appealing to me. Shodoshima Olive Park: good for photos and buying all kinds of souvenirs. About 80% of the visitors are (Taiwanese-speaking) Taiwanese XD It was a filming location for the live-action Kiki's Delivery Service, so there are some facilities for taking photos, and you can rent (magic) brooms for free. Notes Twenty-Four Eyes Movie Village: 8:30 to 17:00, 1,000 yen per person Shodoshima Olive Park: 8:30 to 17:00 Yamaroku wooden-barrel soy sauce For food on Shodoshima, the main specialties are olive oil, somen and soy sauce. I had the olive oil, somen and soy sauce flavors of soft-serve ice cream. The soy sauce one I had at "Yamaroku Shoyu": it's just regular milk flavor with soy sauce poured right on top plus black beans, but surprisingly it goes well together, and I liked it! They even give you a jar of soy sauce to use freely. They brew soy sauce the traditional way in giant barrels made of cedar. You can go inside to look, take photos with the barrels, and there's a simple tour, all free, so when you leave there's a pressure of "I guess I should buy some soy sauce" (I'm thin-skinned...), but I still thought it was well worth it, and that keeping traditions alive really isn't easy. Notes 9:00 to 17:00 20 minutes on foot from the bus stop, soy sauce products from 750 yen. It's a big Japanese-style house, and you can have an ice cream and rest. Moriguni Sake Brewery Another place worth noting is Shodoshima's only sake brewery, "Moriguni Sake Brewery". I came because I really wanted somewhere to rest and there weren't many options (so casual!). By the time I arrived it was 4 in the afternoon, and I only had a cup of sake and a dessert, and sadly didn't get to try the sake lees bread and the food. But the atmosphere was nice (and I was the only customer...!), and I got a great rest. Notes 9:00 to 17:00, closed Thursdays; the bakery is closed Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday Somebody please try their bread on my behalf!!! Wrap-up Overall, the three or four days on Shodoshima were very chill, and the cozy hostel gave me a great first impression. The sights on the island are some very touristy, some very traditional and some natural, and every day you see a different sea view from a different angle. Recommended. (Poor vocabulary.)

title: A Vision Is the Anchor of Life: Reading Be Useful
abstract: What a clear vision gives you: whether a decision is good or bad for you depends on whether it moves you closer to, or further from, the life you want.
text: "Vision" can be what people usually call a goal or a dream: the life you want to live, the person you want to become. It can be vague, and become clear as it narrows down and gets refined through practice. Think about your hopes, your joys and angers, what you like, what you want to pursue, where you'd like to travel, what kinds of people you'd like to meet, what experiences you'd like to have. All of this will shape your future. — Wing, Hunter × Hunter In the old Hunter × Hunter anime, these are the words Wing said to Gon and Killua when they had finished their training at Heavens Arena and were getting ready to leave, and they've stayed with me ever since. In the past I had no concept of a "vision". I just kept searching painfully for a dream, something I wanted to do, a cause to throw myself into, fantasising that once the dream was defined, I'd surely be able to commit to it wholeheartedly and steadily. Fortunately, and unfortunately too, during the long time when I couldn't find a dream, these words were my guiding light. And only after reading Be Useful, and gradually clarifying my dream (or revising it into a more concrete, less cheesy "vision"), did I realise that my vision had been with me all along, deep in my everyday life, and I just hadn't noticed. Here are a few ideas about vision from the book that I think are important: What a clear vision gives you: whether a decision is good or bad for you depends on whether it moves you closer to, or further from, the life you want. Good people know exactly what they're trying to achieve, know how to weigh their choices against their vision, and are very disciplined about it. They review themselves regularly, and as they change, their vision changes too. Stay curious, hunger for information, keep an open mind, and put what you know to use. If you get the chance to read the book, you'll find the author's discipline and persistence seem to go beyond ordinary people. But you could also read it as: he has a very clear and specific vision, and it gives him a strong drive. This post mainly picks out a few important passages from the book, adding my own experience and the things I want to remind myself of. Especially the parts about following through, giving it everything and taking action are exactly what I lack the most. It's a reminder to check whether I'm not trying hard enough, to stop making excuses for myself, and to push myself just a little. (And this time, I'm not pushing myself for someone else, but for me!) Take top athletes as an example. Besides technique, they can visualise the process: they can close their eyes and imagine/see the whole competition. The visualisation of a vision here probably refers to "motor imagery". I've read about it in articles on climbing training, and I also practise it deliberately before climbing, when I study the route and work out my plan (although I rarely do the most basic thing, filming myself to correct my movement). I'm quite curious whether climbing, compared with other sports, naturally needs motor imagery more. Because our stamina is limited, we can't keep getting on the wall to test things with our bodies, so we rely more on trying them out in our imagination. If you don't watch yourself exercise in front of a mirror, you can't know whether your form is correct, whether you have enough muscle, or whether the lines are defined enough. You have to look at yourself properly, objectively and honestly. Only if you're willing to face your mistakes do you have a chance to fix them and get better. You also have to gladly accept your good parts, recognise your strengths and build self-acceptance, and only then do you know how to push yourself in an efficient and effective way, with humility and confidence. People who aren't present get to know you through static poses (a magazine, for example). But the people who do come to see you in person, the ones who matter, observe and judge your every move, and the transitions between those key moments. It's a perfect metaphor. Life isn't only about highlights or big moments. I like the "transitions" mentioned here. The parts that seem unimportant, ordinary, there just to connect things, may be exactly where you're most likely to relax and show a flaw. Could it be that... the "transitions" are how they judge you, and the key to success or failure? And to avoid showing flaws in the small details, "showing your true self" is the easiest choice, rather than playing a role, which takes pretending. Even if you lose by a hair in the end, it doesn't matter, because you've probably done something quite remarkable along the way. It's like not being afraid of failed attempts: even if the final result isn't perfect, or is a failure, something definitely didn't fail. For example, you may not win an Olympic gold medal, but your story of struggle inspires many people to take up and care about that sport. And the perseverance you built as an athlete, even after you become a coach or move to another field, lets you hold on longer and handle pressure better than others. It reminds me of Juhan Shuttai! (重版出來！), a work about a judo athlete who can't keep chasing the Olympic dream because of an injury and switches to working at a publishing house. Both the original manga and the TV drama are great! I also like the later point in the book that "in the gym, every time you push yourself to failure is a kind of failure". It seems imperfect every single time, but actually each time you're closer to your goal. There's no Plan B. Plan B is successfully completing Plan A. ... For every great dream, Plan B is dangerous, because it exists for failure. Rather than telling myself "give it everything!" while carrying out a plan, what I want to remind myself of is, before that, when I'm making the plan: "don't choose the easy road." I'm passionate about following through. ... Important things are often neither simple nor direct, and almost always depend on timing, other people and many variables. Use it or lose it. This is a huge reminder for me, because I'm the king of enthusiasm that lasts three minutes (one of the few things I can say with confidence...). It especially reminded me of everything I've studied in the past: French, Spanish, some investment materials and so on. In the end none of it went anywhere or produced any results, like making a foreign friend because of it, passing a proficiency exam, or investing to create some income. If I ever want to pick it up again, I'll definitely have to review a certain amount from scratch, and all that time is a waste that feels like a pity. I chose to work as a bricklayer because it was like extra weight training. The author mentions he had other jobs, to earn money or to save money for the future. This is worth thinking about. In the best case, "the other job" still helps you reach your vision, but if there's no option that good, be careful not to choose a job that "distracts" you from the vision. I also love this kind of thing myself: "doing one thing that brings multiple benefits". Bricklaying earns money and is also weight training. Or take an example from the later part on helping others: the American writer David Sedaris picks up litter while walking, to the point where a garbage truck was named after him and he had afternoon tea with the Queen of England. Picking up litter while walking means exercising while making the environment better. This has nothing to do with a vision, but while meeting your own needs, if it only costs you a bit of effort, almost no loss to yourself, you can help others and beautify the environment... these accumulate easily and unnoticed into a part of your own gains, even achievements. Doesn't that seem like a good deal? Present your vision to the world as if it has already come true, and it pushes you to start working hard right now, so that it has to come true. An idea of first drawing the big pie in the sky, then forcing yourself to make it real! …review yourself regularly; as you change, your vision changes too.

title: Not Depending on Anyone or Anything: Not in Fandom, Not in Love
abstract: A person can find happiness all on their own: they know what they need, know how to be with themselves, and know how to take care of themselves.
text: Some time ago I met a few Facebook friends I hadn't met before. They chatted about the Korean groups they like and all kinds of fan culture, and the more I listened, the further away it felt from me. Not long after, through work, I came into contact with a music creator. Before we met and worked together, I listened to their work over and over and read interviews, quietly becoming a fan, and after the aura of their live performance I was utterly captivated. Yet inside the sweetness of being a fan, I felt afraid. It's not that I've never been a fan. It's just that when I got happiness out of it, spending days and weeks immersed in collecting information about an idol, I became aware that this kind of dependent craving wasn't appropriate, and chose to cut off the obsession during one "saint mode" episode. I was afraid that "expecting them to work hard at performing and creating to repay your support" would end in disappointment. Fandom is especially one-sided: an idol doesn't have to take responsibility for the feelings you invest, and a hurt heart predictably has nowhere to claim compensation. I've seen quite a few one-sided, dependent relationships: people who make their partner the centre of their life and their top priority, who give their all and sacrifice themselves to maintain the relationship, and who, when they're finally dumped, are left with nowhere to put their resentment. How could they bear the blame of "you put your effort in the wrong direction"? As a friend on the sidelines, I often find it hard to bring up the facts and the problem. Although we say "it takes two to tango" and "every pot has its lid", I still ache for friends whose relationships end sadly. Kusakabe: "(I) can give you everything." Sajo: "No... half is enough." — from Asumiko Nakamura's Sotsugyosei (卒業生) I think it's not only because everyone is an independent individual who can't carry all of the other person, but also because the reason we admire someone is the way they shine, living as themselves, when I'm not around. I'm not free of desire either. I still can't help falling blindly in love; I'm completely an ordinary person with wants and needs. I just consciously avoid putting the centre of my life on someone else. I think a healthy state is that a person can find happiness all on their own: knowing what they need, knowing how to be with themselves, and knowing how to take care of themselves. And going from living alone to living as two should be "1 becomes 2", getting greater happiness, or a different kind of happiness (from being on your own), not "0 becomes 1", where one person isn't happy and only two people are. As Panai said when she sang 〈You're Happy, So I'm Happy〉: Although I've always sung "you're happy, so I'm happy", if one day there's a love that's built on the other person, I mean, that I can only be happy after you're happy. Is that good? I feel it isn't happiness. I feel... maybe it is, I don't know. Timon Studler on Unsplash

title: To My Lost 20-Year-Old Self: A Lifestyle of Pursuing Dreams
abstract: I wrote "A Lifestyle of Pursuing Dreams" in my senior year of university, and the thousand-plus words of drafts never got finished. Back then I wrote down my confusion and guesses about dreams; now I try to answer those guesses with what I've done and gained over the past few years, and to talk with those drafts, with the lost me of that time.
text: A note before we start: I wrote "A Lifestyle of Pursuing Dreams" in my senior year of university. I wrote some, stopped, then wrote some more a few months after graduating and starting work, and the thousand-plus words of drafts never got finished. I think it's time to finish it, using what I've done and gained over the past few years to talk with those drafts, with the lost me of that time. (Well, here I am~) Back then I was writing down my confusion and guesses about dreams, and now I'm trying to give those guesses an answer. I've always liked this title, because it holds two meanings: pursuing "the lifestyle of your dreams" and the lifestyle of "pursuing dreams". "Do I know what the lifestyle I dream of looks like, and pursue it as my goal? Do I know what my dream is, and can I be happy with the lifestyle that comes with pursuing it?" Which one do I actually want? In my senior year, one morning I came home after a night of karaoke (my one and only), looked at the books scattered all over the floor, and my mind was strangely clear. A friend had dropped by the night before and seen the mess in my room laid bare, and it felt like a reminder: "It's time to face your own mess honestly." At the time I shamelessly felt I should take a photo to remember it. Books on planning, theatre, film and art, all sorts of scattered flyers, make-up on a small table, laundry hidden underneath, a handmade cardboard cabinet, folders collecting class notes... these made up me back then. (The bookends from Daiso were still smiling at the scattered books, weren't they.) The theme of university was "lack" I had no skill I could call a specialty, I'd lost interest in developing my department's field, and I lacked the courage to suddenly take a leave of absence or switch departments. So from my second year, for three or four years, I was stuck in "feeling inferior because of lack, and anxious because of feeling inferior", and I even felt guilty about days of relaxing and slacking off without actively improving myself. I didn't know what I liked or wanted to do, and I was full of confusion about the future. So I took many courses in culture, languages and other departments that might interest me, joined off-campus activities in media and education, and read many books from different fields and genres. Through them I found what I was good and bad at, suited and unsuited for, liked and disliked, slowly crossing things off, sorting and summing up, and getting to know myself. Those days of fulfilling learning were happy and solid. Although most of it left no concrete proof of ability (for example, I studied French and Spanish for two years and never took a proficiency test) and didn't help much with job hunting later, in the days after, it quietly helped with my outlook and thinking, academic research, relationships, the fun of daily life (?) and more. But the purpose then was to find, through these attempts, what I really wanted to do and the field I wanted to build expertise in, and in that respect the result was a failure. You could say there was no progress at all With no clear goal or professional strength, job hunting after graduation was painful and confusing. In the end I joined a company related to my major, and convinced myself: "I'll start in the field I'm more professional in, and learn some skills that are useful in other industries too!" I've never known whether that judgement was right or wrong, because the job lasted only a short half year. I did gain practical experience, of course, but didn't leave behind any great achievement that made my résumé shine. The biggest gain was in myself: I deeply realised "it turns out I care a lot about whether the company itself fits my values and ideals, more than pay and benefits, organisational culture or overtime (probably)." Having been through the Sunflower Movement during university, I'd grown the idea of "wanting to change society", but the me back then was small and powerless, and couldn't say concrete methods or directions, so I kept the idea in my heart. I never forgot it, but I was embarrassed to say such a positive, grand idea out loud. One of the reasons I quit decisively was that a university professor nudged me into grad school, and I passed the entrance exam (details in 〈Looking Back | Three Years of Grad School〉, in Chinese). Not wanting to be a full-time grad student, I needed a part-time job, so I looked again at my past experiences, full of variety but without any remarkable results, and suddenly, from an unrelated environmentally friendly habit, an idea flashed: "lifestyle habits = things I believe in; getting others to believe in them too = changing society? Probably... ?" Later, during grad school, I also worked part-time at an environmental foundation. I can't say I did anything great, but several environmental issues have been seen and discussed by more and more people in recent years, so I think I did contribute a tiny bit to changing society. After finishing grad school I left the foundation too (I still felt it wasn't what I most wanted to do). The idea of "wanting to change society" didn't change, only into a smarter-sounding phrase: "wanting to have social impact", a wish as vague as the one back then. My job after graduation was about translating and promoting knowledge. The heavy workload forced me to become a ruthless working machine, painful but happy, until my body sent warning signals, so I turned to answering another guess: "Does 'what I want to do' also include 'the life I want to live'?" The point may not be just "the dream" "...Every day I sleep until I wake naturally. After getting up, I tidy the house a little while waiting for Bin to come back from the fields, then have a leisurely breakfast and read. Then I look at what work I've scheduled for the day, whether it's drawing (拓繪), preparing lessons or writing, and start working while listening to music... So on average I probably work for less than four hours a day... With so little working time, what do I do the rest of the time? The rest of the time I do whatever I want! ... Is the 20-some thousand (NT dollars) enough? In Luye, it's not only enough, there's some left to save..." — Liao Mi, 〈Working Hours for Earning Money〉 (in Chinese) When I wrote "A Lifestyle of Pursuing Dreams", I was probably inspired by Liao Mi's daily-life posts. I found out that this kind of life was possible, and I deeply longed for it. "Maybe... the point isn't only reaching a faraway dream; having a way of life and a rhythm that feels comfortable is important too." Perhaps that's the long-term plan? But tamed by society, I was doubtful about this idea, and kept choosing to try "finding a dream and pursuing it". Yet on this road of testing a hypothesis, testing "can I put up with a certain lifestyle in order to pursue my dream" was much harder and more painful, while exploring "what does the lifestyle of my dreams look like" was relatively easy, and after the pain I took this path. And now I have the lifestyle of my dreams and feel satisfied. Being a freelancer isn't far from Liao Mi's "work very little, and do whatever I want the rest of the time". My income isn't yet enough to be worry-free, and I'm still exploring ways to make this lifestyle last. As for the dream, during these freelance days it has gradually begun to take shape, and I'm slowly working on it in my "do whatever I want" time. But it's not yet the time to talk about it confidently and generously, so I'll stop here for now. Last words Maybe for some people, the days of moving towards a dream and cutting through thorns are what truly feels like living, and that's great too. I once believed that too, and tried to become that kind of person, only to find it didn't suit me. (Maybe it will in the future? At least not now.) In the end, you have to walk it yourself to know what you want and what suits you.

title: Daily Life | Climbing as a Way of Talking to Myself
abstract: Over more than five years of climbing, I've realised a few things along the way, about being alive, about choices, and about what I think of myself.
text: A note before we start: More than 90% of my time is in indoor bouldering gyms, a little in indoor top-roping, and I've only been outdoors (for a class) about 2 times...? I'm a little embarrassed about my lack of progress, but since I'm influenced by different forms of climbing, please allow me to still call it "climbing" in the title. I've now been climbing for over 5 years. About two years ago I wrote down how climbing taught me that "I am who I am, existing has nothing to do with right or wrong, and I don't need to live by other people's standards". This time I want to record some new feelings. I don't know why I photographed an empty view either, but I don't have any other photos on me, so let's go with this. A moment where you can safely practise failing and grow slowly At first I started bouldering just because it was fun, with no goals. In my busy life, my most satisfying state was climbing twice a week: enough to improve a little and still leave time for other hobbies. But because of studies, work, the pandemic, and my shoulders, knees, wrists and other parts getting hurt in turn even though I was already careful, there were also times when I climbed once a week, or once a month. "Climbing can be a way to relieve stress and gives you an endless sense of achievement."...? This is definitely the biggest misjudgement! Maybe after climbing twice a week without a break for two months, you start having magical moments of "I improved again compared to last time!" over and over, but before long you realise that most of the time climbing hovers between "frustration and failure" and "endless starting over". The growth curve doesn't go up all the way (↗) but goes up and down like a wave (〰️), unpredictably. That sounds terrible, and you might even want to equate it with the embarrassing episodes in life you don't want to remember, or with failing to finish a route, or with training hell. In fact, it's an excellent situation where you can fail safely, practise endlessly, debug and learn by trial and error. There's no pressure from a superior grading your performance, no competition or little tricks between colleagues, no exclusion or scheming among peers, so you can put all your attention on yourself. Voilà! Wonderful! And everyone around is an angel, happy to share methods and techniques, cheer loudly for your brave attempts, or be purely delighted when you complete a route. It took me a year and a half to climb V3, and another year and a half to move up to V4. Next to me there are plenty of people who reach V4 within a year, so compared to them I'm well qualified to say I grow slowly. But slow progress doesn't mean slacking off. There's a lot to work on: top rope, leading, technique, reading routes, footwork, strength and endurance training... feeling your breath, the muscles filling with blood, the shifting of your centre of gravity, the friction on your fingertips, and of course learning how to apply force correctly when injured and all kinds of knowledge about the body. The conversation you hear most at a climbing gym: A: "I can't do this one." B: "You can!" Taking my friend L's devastating injury (?) as a warning (though L never stops climbing because of injuries...), I've always climbed in a laid-back way (at least I think so), not obsessed with moving up in "grades" themselves (I still get happy when I do), but breaking down all the important elements of getting stronger and building them up one by one. Even now, before bouldering I still do a 10-minute warm-up and a 10-minute traverse, and climb all the V0s and V1s (this warm-up menu may still be a bit lazy... sweat). I also don't try the same project route too many times (it wears out the same body parts), and I refuse all kinds of risks with an "I'm just bad" spirit. As a result, I climb dynamic routes terribly, underestimate my own ability, and sometimes after egging myself on to try a route I "really can't do", I complete it. Anyway, my grades are occasionally a mess, and my climbing buddies see me as a big bluffer. Climbing is a mirror: you can look bravely, or turn away Across countless attempts, everything you challenge is about yourself: your ability, your fears, your weakness, all the physical or mental things you don't want to admit or can't get past. Here you can try bravely, but it's also fine to choose to give up. Just like my "laid-back" attitude is often an excuse for avoiding problems. For example, I avoid dynamic routes "for fear of injury", but what I'm actually afraid of is stepping out of my comfort zone to learn new things and new sensations, and the frustration that is bound to come with learning. I can avoid it again and again, but the problem will come back again and again, and it's never too late to be brave once on the day I think "I seem to be in good shape today". [System] You've encountered a dynamic route. What will you do? ▶ Fight ▶ Run ▶ ...Next time After I found this pattern in climbing, "I can choose to be brave, I can choose to avoid, I can choose to avoid now and be brave later when I want to", I seemed to be able to face all kinds of conflicts and setbacks in life calmly. For example, when I'm asked to behave against my personality or values, or can't communicate smoothly with a partner, I can choose to adjust myself as if acting (?), or learn other communication skills to start a conversation, but I can also choose not to cooperate and not to compromise, and bravely choose "No! No means no!" Perhaps climbing foretells that "some things I can't do now, I'll still run into later", but at the same time it reminds me to accept the "I just don't want to right now" me, with no need to feel guilty about the choice, let alone blame myself. What returns isn't only the body, but a way of living To perform better on the wall and avoid injury, you can't act on instinct alone, so the body, which I used to use unconsciously and take for granted, became the focus of attention. Practising sensing how every small part of the body works, recognising the nature of fear and weakness, and using all four limbs on the wall feels like getting our animal side back. Civilisation takes us further and further from our bodies, and further from nature. With technology we can go anywhere and no longer need to rely on our feet to move. We can do many things staying inside comfortable and safe man-made buildings. People's lives are easily cut off from nature (or keep only "the parts they think are good"), and the body is often left with only looping labour. This process of getting my body back made it so that I, someone reduced to a useful and efficient part in the great wheel of society, no longer accept the fucking system of "working hard for a better life", no longer want to sacrifice my health and cause permanent damage for work and then use the money I earn to see a doctor. I'm not a professional climber, but when work damages my body and mind more than climbing injuries do, it's a reminder that I should stop and think. (And work takes up as much as 1/3 of the day!) As a human, I should, and deserve to, have a better self and a better life. That's what I think. People were created to be loved, things were created to be used. The reason why the world is in chaos is because things are being loved, and people are being used. — translated from 空屋筆記-免費的自由 (in Chinese) (Although this passage has drifted from its original meaning through repeated quotation, I still like this version.) Making a choice means deciding what to gain and what to lose The calluses on your fingers get soft again after two months of not climbing, but the thickened heels and deformed toes from being curled up in climbing shoes for a long time are almost irreversible. Not long ago, because of a trip abroad and catching COVID, I didn't climb for 4 months. Looking at the usual calluses on my toe joints and the non-congenital bunion on my big toe, I realised: "If I see my body as something sacred and inviolable, but I'm willing to let my toes deform and my body get hurt again and again to keep going, then climbing must be an important choice in my life, right?" I've put in time, money and energy, endured pain and mental torment, and even changed the rules of my life and the order of what matters. (Mental torment: for example, when you're top-roping and your belayer would rather let you "take" for a long time and keep going up than lower you down QQ) Making choices has always been hard for me. I'm afraid of the sunk cost of choosing wrong, of being unable to choose again and stuck, of losing freedom, of having to compromise, yet I know I don't yet know what I want, so I can only keep trying and crossing off what I don't want one by one. As I get older, I seem to be coming to a stage where I can't try things so freely any more, just as when the difficulty of a route rises, the room to adjust your movement gets smaller, and a tiny difference decides whether you get through the crux. So I've realised that the choices I make right now can't be brushed off, and lately I've become much more careful... This is a big task for me, but with all kinds of experience piling up and knowing myself better, I can also feel my direction and goals steadily and clearly narrowing down. I'm not always this harsh on myself though; there are still slacking-off moments of "all roads lead to Rome" when I don't want to choose. Some time ago I picked up the habit of playing the piano again, practising moving to the right chord without looking at my left hand, which is a lot like practising dynamic moves in bouldering. Watching my left hand change chords is like staring at my feet while moving. If you want to improve, you have to find the position with your eyes and remember it with your body: think about the distance between holds, how far and how high to step, and practise over and over. Still, a wrong position on the piano just makes a dissonant note, while in bouldering a dynamic move might mean missing the foothold and twisting a hand. Fear and risk aren't in the same league!

title: Daily Life | Cooking with Carrot Tops
abstract: If you saw carrots with fresh green tops like I did, you probably also wondered, "Is there anything else these beautiful leaves can do besides going beautifully into the food waste bin?" So I tried a few carrot-top dishes.
text: The goal of this round of cooking was "delicious, and the flavour of the greens is easy for anyone to accept". It wasn't only about making a dish and feeling pleased with my zero-waste cooking, but also about keeping in mind the different food preferences of the family eating with me. No. 1: as a seasoning, with roasted carrots "Roasted carrots" is a very common Western side dish: toss them with balsamic vinegar, honey and olive oil at 2:2:1, add salt and pepper to taste, and roast at 200°C for 30–40 minutes, checking and turning the carrots over in between. The key is to get the skin caramelised. The amounts of seasoning and the roasting time depend on the amount and size of the carrots. I like carrots soft enough that a fork goes through easily. My family said it tastes like honey sweet potato! The version with carrot tops is a variation based on NOT ANOTHER COOKING SHOW. First toss the carrots with olive oil, garlic (with the skin on), thyme, salt and pepper and roast them. Then mix olive oil, lemon juice and honey at 2:2:1 with chopped lemon zest, chopped carrot tops (no stems), parsley, salt and pepper, and pour it over the carrots when they come out of the oven. Compared with the previous dish, this one is more of an appetiser: it has more character and is less friendly. The fresh flavour built on greens and lemon seems like something only adults can appreciate, and I believe the carrot tops, as one of the supporting players, can easily be accepted by adults. Roasted carrots that work as an appetiser No. 2: carrot-top salad (a failure) A recipe I found by randomly searching YouTube: chop carrot tops (no stems), tomatoes and garlic, mix with salt, pepper, lemon and orange juice (any citrus works), and you have a raw salad that's easy to serve! First of all, the minced garlic was too spicy, so no matter what, make sure to leave this ingredient out. The rest is very simple: basically a lemon/orange-juice-based salad that doesn't hide the flavour of the carrot tops at all, so people who don't like "grassy" flavours will take three steps back from this salad. And I think most people probably can't accept it... Personally I think a salad is a dish that shows off the original taste of the ingredients, and as an ordinary person I'm not able to make a salad without the original taste of the ingredients (and doesn't that seem a bit like putting the cart before the horse?). People who can enjoy and are willing to try all kinds of "grassy" flavours can give it a go; I'm sure it brings a different salad experience, since you don't often get the chance to eat carrot tops. The unpopular carrot-top salad No. 3: pesto, crowned the best way to use them up The reference recipe is from LOVE&LEMONS. Besides the classic basil leaves and pine nuts, it offers lots of alternatives for the base ingredients of a pesto, including all kinds of leaves and nuts. A very useful article. I added carrot tops, olive oil (quite a lot, because the blender couldn't handle it otherwise), minced garlic, cashews and almonds. The carrot tops don't stand out in the pesto, perhaps because their smell is somewhat softened by the other ingredients. I tried mixing it into a salad as a dressing, but it neither added nor took away anything, a bit boring. After several attempts, I recommend eating it heated. After heating, the garlic flavour clearly comes out and becomes the star. It's great as a spread on baguette slices (I'd add a bit of butter too, super fatty but so satisfying), and as a pasta pesto there's no problem at all: compared to the classic basil pesto it could pass for the real thing, definitely the first choice for using up carrot tops! Pesto pasta (a very awkward moment to take a photo XD) The leaves taken off, the stems thrown away Afterwards After looking up recipes and starting to cook, I found that most of them only use the leaves and still don't use the stems. I did this in the Netherlands. After proudly writing it all down, I realised that carrots bought in Taiwan usually don't come with their tops (I wonder if that's because they're imported, or just the custom after harvesting?), and the variety is different, with thicker stems and leaves, so I'll leave it to the brave to try on Taiwanese carrots XD!

title: Daily Life | You Have to Be Prepared for Cannabis to Help You. Maybe?
abstract: I tried cannabis for the first time and was disappointed to find it didn't have the hallucinogenic effect I'd imagined. Maybe the problem was that I had "no purpose"?
text: This year I gave myself a break and stayed in the Netherlands for three months. As a tourist, I couldn't help wanting to experience "cannabis", which is legal to possess here. This post is mainly a quick record of my experience, and I'll leave the factual stuff to other, more professional articles! Although trying cannabis was on my Netherlands to-do list, I did no research at all at the start. At a dinner in Amsterdam with a friend's friend, I mentioned it, and with their introduction and help I got some. Super basic knowledge, not detailed or professional Cannabis is simply divided into "high" and "sleepy" kinds. With no sleep problems, I naturally said loudly, "I want the high one!" What I bought was joints mixed with tobacco, kept in a plastic bottle like a test tube, about 7 euros a tube. My friend said you can share one with friends, and if you have no friends you can smoke it over several sessions. In any case, it's definitely not meant to be finished all at once. The most basic advice for smoking cannabis is to do it "in a safe place (such as at home), with a trusted friend or family member nearby", because everyone reacts differently, and this guards against danger. As for when to use it, the articles I looked up mention times like after waking up, after work, before a shower, before a movie, before dinner, before sleep and so on, all recommended times to try. Although I got the joints early on, going abroad is a rare chance, I always had lots planned, and the cannabis was forgotten off to the side until two weeks before I went home, when I hurriedly began my smoking project. If you get the chance to try it, I suggest searching for some guide to smoking cannabis first. It always gives first-timers a bit of encouragement (?) and confidence. Is the cannabis senpai really taking me flying? The conclusion first: the effect wasn't obvious on me. At first I was disappointed, and tried to find out which step had gone wrong, asking lots of friends and gradually working it out. In the end I was no longer disappointed. Instead I felt satisfied because I'd learned something, like a child coming across something new. (As an adult, this kind of experience is rare.) I smoked 4–5 times over about two weeks, increasing the dose almost every time and constantly adjusting how I smoked (for someone who has never smoked cigarettes, this takes practice). And to avoid wasting my lovely daytime on the side effect of cannabis (about 2–3 hours after smoking I'd suddenly get extremely sleepy, almost instantly blacking out), I only smoked before movies, before sleep and before cooking. When I asked a born-and-bred Dutch person about the effect of cannabis, he said: "(It's like) when you imagine you're at the beach, you're at the beach." When I talked about it with a friend who had read books on psychedelics, he said: "(Roughly speaking) before psychedelic therapy, you have to prepare, and confirm what the problem and goal are, so that the experience can make sense." The two came together into a reference answer that pointed out my problem: "no purpose". Every time I smoked, it was like handing in homework. I'd take a lighter and the joint out to the balcony, watching the edge of the paper being eaten away by the burning, and thinking, "Did I smoke more this time than last time?" Smoking cannabis looks pretty decadent At first, the only effect I remember is that after smoking I went to cook dinner, and when I was peeling thin green asparagus, it felt like my eyes were a camera with a huge aperture: everything was blurred except the spot I was peeling. I didn't need to focus (= stare hard) or use a short focal length (= bring my eyes close to the object) to get a super depth of field. This feeling was amazing, and you could say it defied physics, right? Next, after smoking I watched a movie, the live-action Thermae Romae starring Hiroshi Abe. Even though I'd read the manga and pretty much knew the plot, I laughed like crazy! Was that the effect of cannabis? I'm not sure! The last experience I only remembered later. While watching Thermae Romae, I opened two special beers. As someone who once tried hard to understand coffee and failed (I can only tell sour from bitter, not floral, fruity, caramel and so on), and who doesn't quite understand beer either (the only thing I've ever said is "this can has more malt flavour, this one is lighter" when drinking two cans at once), I took a sip of one of the beers and said: "This tastes like the smell that hits you when the automatic glass door of an artsy general store opens, and the shop's main colour (the walls and so on) is a misty grey-green." It blew my mind. Was it that the beer itself had a special flavour, or the effect of the cannabis? Although I can't prove whether the last two experiences were affected by cannabis, I feel satisfied. Maybe it's also because almost all my memories of my time in the Netherlands are happy ones! Further reading / references An episode of Explained (流行大百科) on Netflix is about cannabis How to Change Your Mind (Chinese edition, 《改變你的心智》)

title: Unable to Get Closer Because We Don't Understand: Reading 《滌，這個不正常的人》 (Di, This Abnormal Person) #2
abstract: The problem of relationships that can't get closer and can't understand each other is like the elephant in the room that everyone deliberately ignores. And I'm like a hedgehog, always ready to strike back, because showing one vulnerable spot and expressing my real feelings has only ever brought hurt, and I'm too afraid of being hurt again.
text: University, volunteering, internships, grad school, work: after I'd seen many things and made many friends outside, climbed out of my inferiority and felt I should have value, then just when they expected you to become more social through interacting with more people, they felt you'd changed. More extreme, more argumentative, more petty. You point out problems in daily life, change your habits and hold to them, start refusing to join certain activities. All these things I did because I felt I was part of society weren't seen as a positive thing. Do you want to understand me, or change me? Rogers said that people always give "evaluative understanding", for example: "I've had an experience like yours, but my reaction was different from yours." This critical kind of understanding is what people often do: judging others' behaviour that's different from their own, and saying "I understand" and "I know" while doing it, but that's not real "empathy". (p152) Rogers said: "If someone could understand how I really feel, rather than trying to analyse or judge me, then I would surely blossom and grow in that kind of climate." (p153) 'Someone being different from you doesn't mean they're wrong!' (Source: Boys Over Flowers) I've always thought that "making choices" is a matter of personal preference. Sometimes, in order to work with others, we look for reasons to convince them to accept our choice, or we compromise on a choice through negotiation. But why, in my own life, with choices that only affect me, do I still have to cater to the eyes of the world and convince others to accept them? Some people pay expensive rent to live next to the office so they can sleep in a bit; some would rather commute 45 minutes every day to separate work from life. Some want to earn lots of money so they can spend without blinking at any time; some dream of owning a piece of land and living a self-sufficient, ordinary life. These are all just personal preferences with nothing to do with right or wrong. But my choices never won acceptance from my family, and even made me feel like I was being told what to do. This often leaves me confused about my family relationships: because they're family, do I have to accept their values about making choices? What I often feel is evaluative understanding, or unwillingness to understand. I'm not writing this to complain publicly about family relationships or to blame their education of me (in fact I don't), but to talk about something that has long troubled me through the conflict between independent individuals. And in this process I also clearly understand that I'm not the only one in pain, enduring what can't be understood and being denied. They are also enduring my refusal to share, my bad attitude, my polite and distant manner. The problem of relationships that can't get closer and can't understand each other is like the elephant in the room that everyone deliberately ignores. And I'm like a hedgehog, always ready to strike back, because showing one vulnerable spot and expressing my real feelings has only ever brought hurt, and I'm too afraid of being hurt again. Is giving up better? Are you stuck here, and is it all someone else's responsibility? What reason does Mom have to give you money? My tone was a bit harsh. Di listened and then said calmly: "That's easier." (p144) When Di said "that's easier", it also made me think: is giving up all my own persistence and will in front of my family an easier way to keep the peace in the relationship? But is that decision the most "happy" one? Isn't it choosing not to let them know the real me? Accepting that someone will never understand you in their whole life, and choosing to give up communicating and conveying my thoughts, compromising and obeying at every moment of differing opinions, means I've given up making any effort for this relationship. And the only reason I'm "still here" is that we're in a relationship that can't easily be ended. Is that better? Better for whom? In social interactions, we can sometimes dodge, like skiing, the people who crash into us, the things that conflict with us, but the difference is that they are always there. Although until someone changes, we can only keep this uncomfortable status quo, blindfolded and playing minesweeper together, at least I still feel pain, and that's because I still care. I haven't given up. In the process of growing through learning and exploring, I grew my own way of living and my own values, and also the softness to appreciate differences and live with them. I grew a self-centred, mistake-fearing personality that can't relax, and at the same time grew the parts of me that think independently, are careful in what I do, and are likeable. Nature and nurture, choosing to resist or to comply, are woven together in a tangle that's hard to put into words, and they are two sides of the same coin. And because I'm still growing and still practising, I tell myself it's okay.

title: I'm an "Abnormal" Person Too: Reading 《滌，這個不正常的人》 (Di, This Abnormal Person) #1
abstract: Those unbearable "bangs", I've collected many, many of them too. The events themselves don't matter, but "What's there to care about?", "That's your problem." and "It doesn't matter." are the source of every "bang". Like being unable to pass the person carrying a mattress, from things that look small to others I've received a lot of denial and dismissal. And I've been enduring it all along, still enduring.
text: In November 2018, before the election, I was chatting with a senior from grad school about the referendum. She mentioned that I'd always been suppressing my emotions, that my feelings always came like a trickle, and she reminded me to spend some time going back through my childhood memories and looking for the cause, saying this is the starting point of all self-exploration. I'd always thought "I'm normal", but there were those things I could tell were "abnormal reactions", bubbling up constantly like bubbles in boiling water. For example, I felt ashamed and guilty when I decided to drop a course, and had to keep telling myself "it's just a choice, nothing to do with right or wrong." When I made mistakes one after another at work, I'd count "embarrassment one, embarrassment two, embarrassment three" and be afraid of making another, when it really wasn't a big deal. And 《滌，這個不正常的人》 (Di, This Abnormal Person) was a bomb that blew open all my deepest memories. I've collected many unbearable "bangs" too One time you met a person carrying a mattress at the top of the stairs, and you couldn't get past him. You pressed your back against the wall and faced him, waiting for him to pass. ... Hearing this, it seems there was a dividing point in Di becoming "like this". (p139) ... It seems it was also when he was twenty-three, one day he heard a very loud "bang". A very loud "bang", and he said he couldn't stand it any more. That "bang" wasn't the first one he'd encountered, but the thousands-and-hundredth. (p140) Those unbearable "bangs", I've collected many, many of them too. The events themselves don't actually matter, but "What's there to care about?", "That's your problem.", "It doesn't matter." are the source of every "bang". Like being unable to pass the person carrying a mattress, from things that look small to others I've received a lot of denial and dismissal. And I've been enduring it all along, still enduring. At the same time, when it comes to denying your essence, people seem to take it for granted to stick negative labels on it: impulsive, careless, sloppy, doing things my own way, lacking perseverance. If you want to be a good student, you have to erase these wrong personality traits. So I've always worked hard to fix the problem. (There are times I resist too, for example I seem to be doing things my own way more and more?) A four-character comment from primary school at the end of the term (source: the internet) I'm a problem that has to be solved Because I felt "those traits are wrong, and I'm afraid of being denied", I had to hide them so I wouldn't be disliked, and endure the things I disliked and not express my needs so I wouldn't be denied. As a result, when I needed to say my real feelings and needs, I couldn't say them at all: "Will he look down on my dream? Will he find my feelings ridiculous? When I say what I dislike, will he dislike me, and think I'm hard to get along with?" I was too afraid of being denied again, and have always been avoiding the same situation happening again. I'm really good at it. Avoiding people who judge others easily, avoiding situations where I'd have to talk about myself, never saying "I hate" but always saying "I prefer". So last year, when an important friend thought "I'm broken, and should be fixed", it was truly heartbreaking. Even though I know he loves me, he thought it was good for me, and he's a good person. For a while, climbing was repairing my understanding of my personality traits. Like being tall or short, flexible or stiff, in front of a route there's no absolute good or bad, right or wrong; it's all two sides of the same coin. I also learned to recognise the nature of fear, practised facing fear, and practised that failing is okay. (〈What Climbing Taught Me〉 was already written a year and a half ago...!) In the summer of my third year of university, I led a camp in Hualien and Taitung. One night, I went out for a late-night snack and some air with the camp leader at a convenience store. We weren't close yet, and I was easygoing, vague and careful in picking snacks and speaking, but he told me to pick what I liked and always patiently waited for my reply. Once, in the car from Yilan back to Taipei with my supervisor, when I asked him "Am I useless? (and so easily replaced)", he said straight out, "You're important." After I finished the graduation procedures with a senior, she sent me a message: "Good thing you were there today." What I actually needed was just to feel that I was valued. Just to be sure they wouldn't dislike me because of my choices (or hesitation), preferences or troubles.

title: [Daily Life] What Climbing Taught Me
abstract: I first tried bouldering in the spring of 2017, introduced by L.
text: I've decided to use this title that sounds like a primary-school essay! Let me record the process and my feelings. The first time was in March (or April) 2017, introduced by my work partner L. If you see bouldering as a sport, it isn't a fixed, repetitive motion (like running), it's full of variety, and you can do it alone (no partner needed), which suited me perfectly. Suddenly, I, someone who never exercised, had a hobby of "exercising". In July I started a beginner technique class, climbing 2–3 times a week. In October I got hurt for other reasons and took a break, and my bouldering schedule turned into visits to the clinic, and the strength I'd built faded away like past clouds through laziness. In December I learned to belay for top-roping, and after getting my belay certificate in January 2018, I was so busy that I climbed about once a month until June. (Luckily, compared with a driving licence, a belay card is less likely to turn into waste paper.) The cycle of climbing for a while, resting for a while, and falling back to square one made the "useless" label stick painfully to my heart, and I couldn't hide from it, because I'd stuck it on myself. Every cycle I'd break down once, and L would say patiently, "That's just how climbing is." Yes. So is life. Asking and answering myself: "What do you have to complain about?" "Nothing, (can't let go) it's all my problem." August 2018, breaking in climbing shoes, pain and happiness together. In July 2018, I started climbing again. This time, I'd be careful not to get injured, and careful to keep climbing at least once a week. Huge ups and downs in life and in my mood didn't affect keeping to this frequency (...nor did injuries to my knees, ankles and wrists), up to now in 2019. Actually, climbing is a relatively fair thing. In front of a route, as long as you reach the end (complete it), no method is off limits. This also reflects that everyone's physical condition is different, so different methods naturally aren't right or wrong, and nobody criticises your body, because for different routes, being tall is sometimes an advantage and sometimes a disadvantage. Climbing taught me to face myself honestly: my physical condition is what it is, my ability at this stage is what it is, my fears are what they are. Someone else being able to do it doesn't mean I can. If I don't assess honestly, all I end up with is an injury. And about fear, I'm also learning not to run away and to look straight at its existence: afraid of falling, afraid of heights, afraid of getting hurt, afraid of pain... Or sometimes I run away, but I identify what the fear actually is and what my weakness is, find ways to overcome it, and bravely challenge it once the next time I come across it. (And don't compare fears with others; they can't be compared.) Climbing reminds me not to keep counting which parts of my personality I need to change (your personality is like your body: there's no good or bad, right or wrong, it's two sides of the same coin), not to keep blaming myself for my mistakes and imperfections (nobody's perfect), and not to live by other people's standards, trying my best to reach them just because they say "it suits you / you can do it / it has to be you". I should talk to myself honestly: "Do you really like it? Do you want it?" After figuring that out, I should assess it properly with time, resources, health and so on, draw a line of feasibility, and avoid demanding things of myself with baseless high standards. And failing isn't embarrassing, and nobody cares about your failures. You can try with peace of mind, and you don't need to be fully prepared before you act, as long as you make sure you won't suffer harm you can't bear. (As for injury, it always makes me think of "exchange": living is exchanging all the time, risking injury in return for a chance, an experience, to try.) The process of climbing shows that most of my anxiety is actually me trapping myself: setting standards too high, always trying to meet others' expectations, not letting myself rest, and facing problems while injured, a vicious circle.
